## How they got there
Arsenal reached the final as runners-up after losing to Paris Saint-Germain on penalties, finishing with a score of 1-1 and 3-4 on spot kicks. Their path was defined by an exceptional profile where they recorded 3.0 points per game and beat 100% of teams in that season's group phase, alongside a goal difference per game of 2.38 which placed them ahead of all other sides. The team also demonstrated defensive solidity with just 2.8 opponent shots on target per game, better than 97% of their league rivals and 92% of all Champions League teams since 2011-12.

## Would the model have picked them?
The model would have selected Arsenal as a finalist, ranking them second among knockout teams with a 25.6% probability of reaching the final compared to an 8.3% base rate for random participants. Although the model was trained on data from other seasons including later ones and never saw this specific campaign, its expectation aligns closely with reality by identifying the semi-finals as the nearest stage to its calculated value of 1.52. This high ranking indicates that despite not being a top-two pick in every historical context, their statistical profile strongly suggested deep progression.

## Weak spots
The team's performance dipped in areas where they beat fewer than half of the season's teams, most notably committing 13.9 fouls per game which was better than only 11% of their peers. Their approach to ball distribution also showed limitations, with long passes accounting for just 11.4% of all attempts and a total of 450 passes per game, figures that outperformed merely 36% and 39% of teams respectively in the league phase. These metrics highlight specific tactical tendencies where the club lagged behind the majority of its competition during the group stage.

messages.content: You are a football performance analyst writing for a curious, data-literate reader. Use ONLY the facts provided. Quote every number exactly as it appears in the facts, with the same rounding. Do not introduce players, managers, matches, events, analyses or numbers that are not in the facts. 'Teams beaten (%)' figures say how many teams the club did better than on a stat, so higher is always better, including for stats marked '(lower is better)', where doing better means having the lower value. Write them as 'better than X% of teams', never as 'top X%'. SHAP contributions are measured in knockout stages: a positive contribution means the stat pushed the model's expected stage up by that fraction of a round, a negative one pushed it down. A SHAP contribution is the model's view, not a measure of how good the team was at the stat: a team can rank high on a stat the model marked down, so never call a stat a strength or a weakness because of its SHAP sign. Everything here is a statistical association, not a cause: never say a stat or a team's profile drove, powered, propelled, carried, helped, hindered or prevented a result, and do not explain why a stat got its contribution. Use 'significant' or 'significantly' only for a Holm-adjusted p-value comparison, never for other differences. Write plain markdown without tables.
